rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The theophany had two effects: the mountain shattered into pieces and Moses fell unconscious.
rows.anchor: ترتب على التجلي أمران أحدهما تفتت الجبل وتفرق أجزائه، والثاني خرور موسى مغشيا عليه

rows.speaker: ابن زيد وجماعة المفسرين
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and a group of exegetes say Moses fainted, rather than died; the wording that he later came to is evidence against death.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن زيد وجماعة المفسرين، وقال السدي ميتا ويبعده لفظة أفاق

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Moses fell dead, a view weakened by the verse's saying that he came to.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي ميتا ويبعده لفظة أفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interpreting the theophany as bodily appearance is impossible for God.
rows.anchor: والتجلي بمعنى الظهور الجسماني مستحيل على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقوم
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others say the mountain crumbled when God's light fell upon it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وقوم لما وقع نوره عليه تدكدك

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad interprets the disclosure as the mountain seeing so much of God's dominion that it crumbled.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: المعنى ظهر للجبل من ملكوت الله ما تدكدك به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that a portion of the Throne appeared to the mountain, which collapsed from awe.
rows.anchor: وقيل ظهر جزء من العرش للجبل فتصرع من هيبته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations say God's command appeared, or that He appeared to the mountain's people, meaning Moses and the seventy with him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ظهر أمره تعالى، وقيل: تجلى لأهل الجبل يريد موسى والسبعين الذين معه

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says God showed a tiny amount of the light behind the veils, compared to a bull's nostril.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: أظهر الله من نور الحجب مثل منخر الثور

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن سلام وكعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Salam and Ka'b al-Ahbar say the mountain received only a needle's-eye amount of God's majesty.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله بن سلام: وكعب الأحبار ما تجلى من عظمة الله للجبل إلا مثل سم الخياط

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says God's power appeared to Moses and His command and will confronted him.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فلما ظهر له اقتداره وتصدى له أمره وإرادته

rows.speaker: القاضي أبي بكر بن الطيب وغيره
rows.claim: Some theologians say God created life, sensation, and perception in the mountain; it perceived His disclosure and crumbled from the overwhelming sight, while Moses fainted.
rows.anchor: إن الله خلق للجبل حياة وحسا وإدراكا يرى به ثم تجلى له أي ظهر وبدا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The interpretation that God gave the mountain perception before the theophany is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وهذا المعنى مروي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading attributes the theophany to God in a manner befitting Him, without movement or any description implying corporeality.
rows.anchor: والظاهر نسبة التجلي إليه تعالى على ما يليق به من غير انتقال ولا وصف يدل على الجسمية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the mountain became dust.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس صار ترابا

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the mountain became scattered pieces.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل قطعا متفرقة

rows.speaker: أنس عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Anas reports from the Messenger that the mountain became six mountains: Uhud, Warqan, and Radwa near Medina, and Thawr, Thabir, and Hira near Mecca.
rows.anchor: وقيل صار ستة أجبل ثلاثة بالمدينة أحد وورقان ورضوى، وثلاثة بمكة ثور وثبير وحراء، رواه أنس عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts say only the mountain's top disappeared, or it became dust scattered by the winds.
rows.anchor: وقيل ذهب أعلاه وبقي أسفله، وقيل صار غبارا تذروه الرياح

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan reports that the mountain flowed through the earth and reached the sea beneath the layers of earth.
rows.anchor: قال سفيان: روي أنه انساح في الأرض وأفضى إلى البحر الذي تحت الأرضين

rows.speaker: ابن الكلبي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Kalbi says the mountain continues descending into that sea until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الكلبي: فهو يهوي فيه إلى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority interpret dakk as crushed or as having been made into a level expanse.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور دكا أي مدكوكا أو ذا دك

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read dakāʾ, meaning flat ground, likened to a she-camel without a hump.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي دكاء على وزن حمراء والدكاء الناقة التي لا سنام لها

rows.speaker: الربيع بن خيثم
rows.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Khaytham cites the phrase 'extend your hand dakāʾ' to mean stretching it evenly.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع بن خيثم: ابسط يدك دكاء أي مدها مستوية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari defines dakka as a raised hill; this suits the view that the top vanished while most of the mountain remained.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري والدكاء اسم للرابية الناشزة من الأرض كالدكة

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Waththab reads dakk, taking it as pieces, a plural patterned like ghuzz from ghazaʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يحيى بن وثاب دكا أي قطعا جمع دكاء نحو غز جمع غزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dakkā is accusative as the second object of jaʿalahu; al-Akhfash's analysis as an absolute object like julūsan is weak.
rows.anchor: وانتصب على أنه مفعول ثان لجعله ويضعف قول الأخفش إن نصبه من باب قعدت جلوسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ṣaʿiqan describes Moses' simultaneous state; the verb form ṣaʿiqahu/ṣaʿiqa is among verbs whose transitivity changes with vowel movement.
rows.anchor: وصعقا حال مقارنة، ويقال صعقه فصعق وهو من الأفعال التي تعدت بالحركة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense is that neither Moses nor the mountain could bear seeing God at the theophany, so the mountain crumbled and Moses fainted.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن موسى والجبل لم يطيقا رؤية الله تعالى حين تجلى فلذلك اندك الجبل وصعق موسى

rows.speaker: عياض بن موسى عن القاضي أبي بكر بن الطيب
rows.claim: Iyad transmits from al-Qadi Abu Bakr that Moses saw God and fainted, while the mountain saw its Lord and crumbled after God enabled it to perceive Him.
rows.anchor: أن موسى اليه السلام رأى الله فلذلك خر صعقا وأن الجبل رأى ربه فلذلك صار دكا

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Shayba reports Ka'b saying God divided speech and sight between Muhammad and Moses: He spoke to Moses twice, while Muhammad saw Him twice.
rows.anchor: وذكر وأبو بكر بن أبي شيبة عن كعب قال إن الله تعالى قسم كلامه ورؤيته بين محمد وموسى

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes recount descriptions and counts of Muhammad's visions of the seven heavens' angels and the Throne bearers, but the author says God knows their soundness.
rows.anchor: وذكر المفسرون من رؤيته ملائكة السموات السبع وحملة العرش وهيئاتهم وأعدادهم ما الله أعلم بصحته

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Moses' words of repentance were for asking to see God in this world.
rows.anchor: أي من مسألة الرؤية في الدنيا قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani transmits that Moses repented for asking about the vision before receiving permission.
rows.anchor: أو من سؤالها قبل الاستئذان أو عن صغائري حكاه الكرماني

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says this was customary turning to God when a believer sees overwhelming signs, not repentance for a particular act.
rows.anchor: أشار إليه ابن عطية، وقال الزمخشري قال سبحانك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads Moses as declaring God transcendent of anything impermissible, including the vision, and repenting for seeking it.
rows.anchor: أنزهك عن ما لا يجوز عليك من الرؤية وغيرها تبت إليك من طلب الرؤية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari answers that Moses repented for uttering the great request without God's permission, even though his intention was sound.
rows.anchor: عن إجرائه تلك المقالة العظيمة وإن كان لغرض صحيح على لسانه من غير إذن فيه من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari argues that the verse magnifies the vision: the mountain shook and was crushed, its seekers were struck down, and Moses also repudiated the request and turned to God.
rows.anchor: وكيف أرجف الجبل بطالبيها وجعله دكا وكيف أصعقهم ولم يخل كليمه من نفيان ذلك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari attacks Sunnis for accepting the vision and says their appeal to bilā kayf conceals an incoherent belief.
rows.anchor: كيف اتخذوا هذه العظيمة مذهبا ولا يغرنك تسترهم بالبلكفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author identifies al-Zamakhshari's treatment as a Mu'tazilite interpretation and a habitual insult against Sunnis.
rows.anchor: وهو تفسير على طريقة المعتزلة وسب لأهل السنة والجماعة على عادته

rows.speaker: بعض العدلية
rows.claim: A Mu'tazilite poet ridicules a group calling its own desires Sunnah and accuses Sunnis of likening God to creation while hiding behind bilā kayf.
rows.anchor: لجماعة سموا هواهم سنة ... وجماعة حمر لعمري مؤكفه

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر أحمد بن إبراهيم بن الزبير
rows.claim: Abu Ja'far transmits a Sunni counter-poem accusing the earlier poet of ignorant slander against the Umma and of throwing false accusations.
rows.anchor: شبهت جهلا صدر أمة أحمد

rows.speaker: قطرب وابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Qutrub and Ibn al-Anbari explain the poetic phrase as a house whose supports are strong and tall.
rows.anchor: بيتا دعائمه أعز وأطول أي عزيزة طويلة قاله قطرب وابن الأنباري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that interpretation, the people are to take the good of the scripture that earns reward and avoid its prohibitions that bring punishment.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا أمروا بأن يأخذوا بحسنها وهو ما يترتب عليه الثواب دون المناهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposal that aḥsan is merely an extra connective meaning 'take it' is weak, since nouns are not added without meaning.
rows.anchor: وقيل أحسن هنا صلة والمعنى يأخذوا بها وهذا ضعيف لأن الأسماء لا تزاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʾkhudhū is jussive as the response to the command; the command to Moses must be construed as an instruction to tell his people so that command and response cohere.
rows.anchor: وانجزم يأخذوا على جواب الأمر وينبغي تأويل وأمر قومك لأنه لا يلزم من أمر قومه

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i's alternative makes yaʾkhudhū jussive through an understood imperative lām, since telling the people means telling them to take it.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن كون قوله يأخذوا مجزوما على إضمار لام الأمر أي ليأخذوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One grammatical possibility supplies an omitted object: they should make themselves adhere to the best of the scripture.
rows.anchor: ومفعول يأخذوا محذوف لفهم المعنى أي يأخذوا أنفسهم بأحسنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility treats the preposition bāʾ as extra, so the command means to take the best of the scripture directly.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون الباء زائدة أي يأخذوا أحسنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers that bāʾ attach to yaʾkhudhū while serving both the command to Moses and the people's taking, by the rule of the second governor.
rows.anchor: والوجه الأول أحسن وانظر إلى اختلاف متعلق الأمرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses is told to take all the scripture forcefully, while his people are told only to take its best parts without emphasis; prophetic office carries a stricter duty, as shown by Muhammad's night prayer obligation.
rows.anchor: أمر موسى بأخذ جميعها، فقيل: فخذها بقوة وأكد الأخذ بقوله بقوة وأمروا هم أن يأخذوا بأحسنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here seeing means eyesight, which accounts for the verb taking two objects.
rows.anchor: والإراءة هنا من رؤية العين ولذلك تعدت إلى اثنين

rows.speaker: علي وقتادة ومقاتل وعطية العوفي
rows.claim: Ali, Qatada, Muqatil, and Atiyya al-Awfi identify the abode of the wrongdoers as Egypt, and Pharaoh and his people as the wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: دار الفاسقين مصر قاله علي وقتادة ومقاتل وعطية العوفي والفاسقون فرعون وقومه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the land was emptied and destroyed because of its people's sin, as a warning against repeating their sin and suffering their punishment.
rows.anchor: كيف أقفرت منهم ودمروا لفسقهم لتعتبروا فلا تفسقوا مثل فسقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says the sea cast Pharaoh and his people ashore after drowning, allowing the Israelites to see where the wrongdoers died.
rows.anchor: أنه لما أغرق فرعون وقومه أوحى إلى البحر أن اقذف أجسادهم إلى الساحل

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the people saw the sites of destroyed peoples such as ʿAd and Thamud as they traveled past them.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: ما مروا عليه إذا سافروا من مصارع عاد وثمود والقرون الذين أهلكوا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada also identifies the abode as Syria and the people as the Amalekites Moses was ordered to fight.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة أيضا الشام والمراد العمالقة الذين أمر موسى بقتالهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد والحسن
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Hasan say the abode is Hell and the wrongdoers are those who disbelieved in Moses and other messengers.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد والحسن: دار الفاسقين جهنم والمراد الكفرة بموسى وغيره

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets seeing as knowing by the heart: God will teach the Israelites the earlier peoples' histories and punishments.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: سأريكم من رؤية القلب أي سأعلمكم سير الأولين وما حل بهم من النكال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the abode as the wrongdoers' eventual fate, knowable only through reports; the author says this is close to Ibn Zayd's view.
rows.anchor: وقيل دار الفاسقين أي ما دار إليه أمرهم وهذا لا يدرك إلا بالأخبار التي يحدث عنها العلم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya argues that if the vision is inward knowledge, the causative verb should take a third object; an omitted predicate is not permitted or would be ugly in scripture.
rows.anchor: ولو كان من رؤية القلب لتعدى بالهمزة إلى ثلاثة ولو قال قائل المفعول الثالث يتضمنه المعنى فهو مقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Ibn Atiyya's restriction: an object in the aʿlama construction can be omitted when context supplies it, including a predicate, and the original subject-predicate structure does not bar ellipsis.
rows.anchor: وحذف المفعول الثالث في باب أعلم لدلالة المعنى عليه جائز

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads saʾurīkum with a still wāw after the hamza; Abu al-Fath explains it as an extended ḍamma suited to the verse's threat, while the author calls that weak because extension belongs to poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن: سأريكم بواو ساكنة بعد الهمزة على ما يقتضيه رسم المصحف ووجهت هذه القراءة بوجهين

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح
rows.claim: Abu al-Fath explains the still wāw as lengthening the ḍamma into a wāw, an effect he says suits the verse's warning and severity.
rows.anchor: قال: ويحسن احتمال الواو في هذا الموضع أنه موضع وعيد وإغلاظ فمكن الصوت فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Abu al-Fath's explanation because vowel extension is properly a poetic license.
rows.anchor: وهذا التوجيه ضعيف لأن الإشباع بابه ضرورة الشعر

rows.speaker: الأخوان والشعبي وابن وثاب والجحدري وابن مصرف والأعمش وأيوب
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i, al-Shaʿbi, Ibn Waththab, al-Jahdari, Ibn Masraf, al-Aʿmash, and Ayyub read ḥilyihim with a kasra on ḥāʾ following the lām.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان من حليهم بكسر الحاء إتباعا لحركة اللام كما قالوا: عصى

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة والحسن وأبو جعفر وشيبة
rows.claim: The remaining canonical readers, al-Hasan, Abu Jaʿfar, and Shayba read ḥuliyyihim with a ḍamma; it is a plural on the fuʿūl pattern with vowel assimilation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة والحسن وأبو جعفر وشيبة بضم الحاء وهو جمع حلي نحو ثدي وثدي

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqub reads ḥilyihim with a fatḥa and still lām, a singular used generically or a collective noun like tamr/tamra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يعقوب من حليهم بفتح الحاء وسكون اللام وهو مفرد يراد به الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ornaments may be attributed to the Israelites because they became booty from Pharaoh's drowned people and Aaron collected them for Moses to decide about.
rows.anchor: إما لكونهم ملكوه من ما كان على قوم فرعون حين غرقوا ولفظهم البحر فكان كالغنيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, they had been Israelites' wealth seized by the Copts as tax, which the Israelites recovered through a loan arrangement.
rows.anchor: أو ملكوه إذ كان من أموالهم التي اغتصبها القبط بالجزية التي كانوا وضعوها عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if they did not own the jewelry, its genitive attribution is valid because their hands handled it as a loan.
rows.anchor: وإما لكونهم لم يملكوه لكن تصرفت أيديهم فيه بالعارية فصحت الإضافة إليهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Sallam transmits from al-Hasan that the Israelites borrowed the jewelry from the Copts for a wedding; another account says for a feast day.
rows.anchor: روى يحيى بن سلام عن الحسن: أنهم استعاروا الحلي من القبط لعرس، وقيل: ليوم زينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Pharaoh's people died, the jewelry remained with the Israelites; Aaron ordered it gathered as a loan to be returned and entrusted it to the goldsmith Samaritan, who cast the calf.
rows.anchor: فأمر هارون مناديا برد العارية ليرى فيها موسى رأيه إذا جاء فجمعه وأودعه هارون عند السامري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says the jewelry was not returned because the Copts might discover the Israelites' secret departure, which God had ordered Moses to undertake.
rows.anchor: وقيل: منعهم من رد العارية خوفهم أن يطلع القبط على سراهم إذ كان تعالى أمر موسى أن يسري بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ʿijl is a young calf, and jasad means a lifeless body; other views define the calf as a headless body of solid gold or as hollow.
rows.anchor: والعجل ولد البقرة القريب الولادة ومعنى جسدا جثة جمادا، وقيل: بدنا بلا رأس ذهبا مصمتا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says jasad means a body with flesh and blood like ordinary bodies.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: جسدا بدنا ذا لحم ودم كسائر الأجساد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the Samaritan took dust from the trace of Gabriel's horse at the sea crossing and threw it into the calf, making it low.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: إن السامري قبض قبضة من تراب من أثر فرس جبريل عليه السلام يوم قطع البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls the flesh-and-blood account weak: reports say Moses filed the calf down and threw it into the sea, which fits metal, not flesh.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف أعني كونه لحما ودما لأن الآثار وردت بأن موسى برده بالمبارد وألقاه في البحر

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says calling it a body indicates that it had no soul.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: ذكر الجسد دلالة على عدم الروح فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording that the calf lowed appears to indicate life, because only a living thing lows.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله له خوار يدل على أنه فيه روح لأنه لا يخور إلا ما فيه روح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says the hollow calf had specially shaped pipes inside, placed in the wind so air created a lowing-like sound.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لما صنعه أجوف تحيل لتصويته بأن جعل في جوفه أنابيب على شكل مخصوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says someone concealed beneath it blew into it so the sound seemed to come from inside.
rows.anchor: وقيل: جعل تحته من ينفخ فيه من حيث لا يشعر به فيسمع صوت من جوفه كالخوار

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani says a hidden boy was put inside the calf and lowed on a signal by opening and closing a chamber in its belly.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني: جعل في بطن العجل بيتا يفتح ويغلق فإذا أراد أن يخور أدخله غلاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further possibility is that God caused the calf to low as a test for the Israelites.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يحتمل أن يكون الله أخاره ليفتن بني إسرائيل وخواره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed image behind the idiom has people bowing their heads and resting their chins on their hands, in a posture where removing the hand would make them fall face-first.
rows.anchor: يطأطىء رأسه ويضع ذقنه على يده معتمدا عليها ويصبر على هيئة لو نزعت يده لسقط على وجهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here fī can mean ʿalā, so 'in their hands' means 'on their hands,' as in the phrase about crucifixion in palm trunks.
rows.anchor: ومعنى في أيديهم أي على أيديهم كقوله ولأصلبنكم في جذوع النخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the passive s-qu-ṭ idiom, the prepositional phrase stands in the agent position because hands are the instrument of grasping and control.
rows.anchor: وكان متعلق سقط قوله في أيديهم لأن اليد هي الآلة التي يؤخذ بها ويضبط وسقط مبني للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive construction can be illustrated by ordinary phrases such as sitting in a house or laughing at someone.
rows.anchor: كما تقول: جلس في الدار وضحك من زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that s-qu-ṭ here contains an object meaning the source 'casting down' is corrected: the implied object should be a pronoun for the verbal noun 'falling,' not the noun itself as an unexpressed agent.
rows.anchor: وصوابه وهو هنا ضمير المصدر الذي هو السقوط لأن سقط ليس مصدر الإسقاط

rows.speaker: ابن السميقع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sumayqiʿ and a group read saqaṭa in the active voice rather than the passive.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة منهم ابن السميقع سقط في أيديهم مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari glosses the idiom as grief falling into their hands.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري أي وقع الغض فيها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says regret fell into their hands.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: سقط الندم في أيديهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the meaning could be that loss and disappointment fell into their hands.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ويحتمل أن الخسران والخيبة سقط في أيديهم

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Abla reads usqiṭa in the passive fourth form, and takes raʾaw as meaning that they realized they had gone astray.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة: أسقط في أيديهم رباعيا مبنيا للمفعول ورأوا أي علموا أنهم قد ضلوا

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi proposes reversing the order: first they realized their error, then remorse fell upon them because of their great sorrow.
rows.anchor: يجب أن يكون المؤخر مقدما لأن الندم والتحسر إنما يقعان بعد المعرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says no reversal is needed: uncertainty about whether an action was right can cause regret before reflection establishes that it was wrong.
rows.anchor: ولا يحتاج إلى هذا التقدير بل يمكن تقدم الندم على تبين الضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their plea for mercy turns wholly to God and acknowledges the enormity of what they did.
rows.anchor: قالوا: لئن لم يرحمنا ربنا انقطاع إلى الله تعالى واعتراف بعظيم ما أقدموا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because calf worship was the greatest sin, they begin by asking for mercy, which encompasses all things and leads to forgiveness; Adam and Eve instead first asked forgiveness after the direct rebuke over the forbidden tree.
rows.anchor: ولما كان هذا الذنب وهو اتخاذ غير الله إلها أعظم الذنوب بدؤوا بالرحمة التي وسعت كل شيء

rows.speaker: الأخوان والشعبي وابن وثاب والجحدري وابن مصرف والأعمش وأيوب
rows.claim: These readers use second-person verbs in the plea and address God directly as Lord.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان والشعبي وابن وثاب والجحدري وابن مصرف والأعمش وأيوب بالخطاب في ترحمنا وتغفر ونداء ربنا

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة ومجاهد والحسن والأعرج وأبو جعفر وشيبة بن نصاح
rows.claim: The remaining canonical readers and named authorities use third-person verbs, with rabbunā in the nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة ومجاهد والحسن والأعرج وأبو جعفر وشيبة بن نصاح وغيرهم: يرحمنا ربنا ويغفر لنا بالياء فيهما

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy's codex places rabbunā before the conditional plea as an address, then uses second-person verbs.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف أبي قالوا: ربنا لئن ترحمنا وتغفر لنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two forms may have been spoken in succession by everyone or by separate groups: the fearful addressed God directly, while the embarrassed spoke indirectly.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون القولان صدرا منهم جميعهم على التعاقب أو هذا من طائفة وهذا من طائفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their repeated address as Lord is a fine appeal because the Lord owns, cares for, and repairs what is corrupted among His servants.
rows.anchor: وفي قولهم: ربنا استعطاف حسن إذ الرب هو المالك الناظر في أمر عبيده والمصلح منهم ما فسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses returned from his communion with God to his people angry and sorrowful; when he confirmed their devotion to the calf, he cast down the tablets.
rows.anchor: ولما رجع موسى إلى قومه غضبان أسفا قال بئسما خلفتموني من بعدي أعجلتم أمر ربكم أي رجع من المناجاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Moses heard the Israelites' sounds near their camp, called them idle people, then became angry and sorrowful when he found them worshiping the calf.
rows.anchor: يروى أنه لما قرب من محلة بني إسرائيل سمع أصواتهم فقال هذه أصوات قوم لاهين

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says God informed Moses before he returned that his people had been seduced by the calf, explaining his anger; the author links this to the verse in Ta-Ha.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري أخبره تعالى قبل رجوعه أنهم قد فتنوا بالعجل فلذلك رجع وهو غاضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghaḍbān is an intensive form; anger is the heart boiling because something painful has happened.
rows.anchor: وغضبان من صفات المبالغة والغضب غليان القلب بسبب حصول ما يؤلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accounts say Moses was among the quickest to anger and also quick to recover.
rows.anchor: وذكروا أنه عليه السلام كان من أسرع الناس غضبا وكان سريع الفيئة

rows.speaker: ابن القاسم عن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qasim says he heard Malik report that smoke rose from Moses' cap and his body hair stood over his garment when he was angry.
rows.anchor: قال ابن القاسم: سمعت مالكا يقول كان إذا غضب طلع الدخان من قلنسوته ورفع شعر بدنه جبته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi interpret asaf as sorrowful.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن عباس والحسن والسدي أو الجزع قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets asaf as distress or agitation.
rows.anchor: أو الجزع قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري وابن عطية
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya say asaf can mean grieving or intensely angry, and it most often means sorrowful.
rows.anchor: أو المتلهف أو الشديد الغضب قاله الزمخشري وابن عطية قال: وأكثر ما يكون بمعنى الحزين

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba gives angered and regretful as additional meanings of asaf.
rows.anchor: أو المغضب قاله ابن قتيبة أو النادم قاله القتبي أيضا

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says the meanings of asaf are close: what comes from someone below angers, while what comes from someone above causes grief.
rows.anchor: أو متقاربان قاله الواحدي قال: فإذا أتاك ما تكره ممن دونك غضبت أو ممن فوقك حزنت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The calf worship angered Moses, while God's having tested his people grieved him, as God had already told him.
rows.anchor: فأغضبه عبادتهم العجل وأحزنه فتنة الله إياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke 'you took my place badly' may address the Samaritan and calf worshipers for substituting the calf for worship of God, or Israel's leaders, including Aaron and believers, for failing to stop the idolatry.
rows.anchor: والخطاب إما للسامري وعباد العجل أي بئسما قمتم مقامي حيث عبدتم العجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'after me' means after Israel had witnessed Moses' monotheism, or after he had taught them monotheism and restrained their desires to worship cattle.
rows.anchor: وخلفتموني يدل على البعدية في الزمان والمعنى هنا من بعد ما رأيتم مني توحيد الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A successor is expected to follow the predecessor's way; khalafahu bi-khayr or bi-sharr means he did good or evil after the predecessor left.
rows.anchor: ومن حق الخلف أن يسير سيرة المستخلف ولا يخالفه ويقال خلفه بخير أو شر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿajiltum is a rebuking question.
rows.anchor: أعجلتم استفهام إنكار

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains ʿajila ʿan as leaving an affair unfinished; the causative form means making someone hurry away and implies outstripping the appointed time.
rows.anchor: يقال: عجل عن الأمر إذا تركه غير تام ونقيضه تم عليه وأعجله عنه غيره ويضمن معنى سبق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads Moses as accusing them of abandoning the wait for God's command and covenant, assuming his appointed time had ended and he had died, then changing religion like earlier nations.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أعجلتم عن أمر ربكم وهو انتظار موسى حافظين لعهده وما وصاكم به

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reports that the Samaritan told them the calf was their and Moses' god and Moses would not return because he had died.
rows.anchor: وروي أن السامري قال لهم أحين أخرج إليهم العجل هذا إلهكم وإله موسى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya interprets the question as asking whether they tried to outpace God's decree and hastened Moses' arrival before the appointed time.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: معناه أسابقتم قضاء ربكم واستعجلتم إتياني من قبل الوقت الذي قدرته

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqub distinguishes ʿajiltu al-shayʾ, being ahead of a thing, from aʿjaltu al-rajul, making a person hurry.
rows.anchor: وقال يعقوب: يقال عجلت الشيء سبقته وأعجلت الرجل استعجلته أي حملته على العجلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations take the question to mean that they hastened God's forty-night appointment, His wrath, or their worship of the calf.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه أعجلتم ميعاد ربكم أربعين ليلة، وقيل: أعجلتم سخط ربكم، وقيل: أعجلتم بعبادة العجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Haste means advancing something before its proper time and is blameworthy, unlike the praised promptness in Moses' words 'I hastened to You, Lord, to please You.'
rows.anchor: وقيل: العجلة التقدم بالشيء في غير وقته، قيل: وهي مذمومة ويضعفه قوله وعجلت إليك رب لترضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tablets were the Torah; Moses, carrying them, set them down in anger at the calf worship and zeal for God's religion.
rows.anchor: وألقى الألواح وأخذ برأس أخيه يجره إليه أي الألواح التوراة وكان حاملا لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites reportedly loved Aaron more than Moses because Aaron had a gentler disposition.
rows.anchor: وقالوا كان هارون ألين منه خلقا ولذلك كان أحب إلى بني إسرائيل منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Moses dropped the tablets in shock at what had happened to his people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ألقاها دهشا لما دهمه من أمرهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the tablets broke when Moses dropped them; he recovered the greater part containing detailed knowledge, while the remaining piece held guidance and mercy.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: أن موسى عليه السلام لما ألقاها تكسرت فرفع أكثرها الذي فيه تفصيل كل شيء

rows.speaker: جماعة من المفسرين
rows.claim: A group of exegetes say six sevenths of the tablets were taken up and one seventh remained.
rows.anchor: وروي أنها رفع ستة أسباعها وبقي سبع قاله جماعة من المفسرين

rows.speaker: أبو الفرج بن الجوزي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Jawzi says it is unsound that Moses threw the tablets in a way that broke them.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الفرج بن الجوزي لا يصح أنه رماها رمي كاسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Moses merely set the tablets down: his hands had to be free to seize Aaron, and the later statement that he took them again shows they neither broke nor lost portions.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه ألقاها من يديه لأنهما كانتا مشغولتين بها وأراد إمساك أخيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of taking Aaron by the head is that Moses actually grasped and pulled his head toward him.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه أخذ برأسه أي أمسك رأسه جاره إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views say Moses took Aaron by his hair, locks and beard, beard alone, or ear, or only gestured rather than physically seizing him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بشعر رأسه، وقيل: بذوائبه ولحيته، وقيل: بلحيته، وقيل: بأذنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author supports this explanation by pointing to the later account of Moses anger subsiding.
rows.anchor: ويدل على هذا الظاهر قوله: ولما سكت عن موسى الغضب وقوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent explanation is that Moses seized Aaron in anger at his failure to prevent calf worship despite being appointed over the Israelites and commanded to reform them.
rows.anchor: والظهر أن سبب هذا الأخذ هو غضبه على أخيه وكيف عبدوا العجل وهو قد استخلفه فيهم وأمره بالإصلاح وأن لا يتبع سبيل من أفسد

rows.speaker: هارون
rows.claim: Aaron's appeal that Moses not seize him by beard or head, and his fear of dividing Israel, is quoted from Ta-Ha.
rows.anchor: إني خشيت أن تقول فرقت بين بني إسرائيل ولم ترقب قولي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Moses dragged Aaron by the hair and locks in the shock of the event, suspecting Aaron had failed to restrain the people.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: أي بشعر رأسه يجره إليه بذوائبه وذلك لشدة ما ورد عليه من الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says Moses grabbed Aaron only to tell him privately that the tablets had descended during his communion, and Aaron stopped him lest the Israelites mistake the private exchange for humiliation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ذلك الأخذ والجر كان ليسر إليه أنه نزل عليه الألواح في مناجاته وأراد أن يخفيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Moses pulled Aaron close to learn what happened; Aaron feared the Israelites would think Moses was humiliating him and explained their oppression.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ضمه ليعلم ما لديه فكره ذلك هارون لئلا يظنوا إهانته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats the gesture as affection rather than insult, like Arabs seizing a brother's beard.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان ذلك على سبيل الإكرام لا على سبيل الإهانة كما تفعل العرب من قبض الرجل على لحية أخيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron addresses Moses as 'son of my mother' to plead weakness and tenderness; Arabs commonly invoke the mother to soften a brother, as in cited poetry.
rows.anchor: ناداه نداء استضعاف وترفق وكان شقيقه وهي عادة العرب تتلطف وتتحنن بذكر الأم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source says their mother was a believer, while their father was cut off from kin by disbelief, as in God's statement to Noah.
rows.anchor: وأيضا فكانت أمهما مؤمنة قالوا: وكان أبوه مقطوعا عن القرابة بالكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron invoked their mother because her right was greater through the hardship of bearing, raising, and caring for him.
rows.anchor: وأيضا لما كان حقها أعظم لمقاساتها الشدائد في حمله وتربيته والشفقة عليه ذكره بحقها

rows.speaker: الحرميان وأبو عمرو وحفص
rows.claim: The two Medinan readers, Abu Amr, and Hafs read ibn umma with a fatḥa on mīm; the Kufans analyze it as the shortened form of yā ibn ummāh and an inflected possessive.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحرميان وأبو عمرو وحفص: ابن أم بفتح الميم، فقال الكوفيون: أصله يا ابن أماه

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh analyzes ibn umma with an open mīm as two nouns compounded and built on fatḥa, rather than a genitive possessive.
rows.anchor: وقال سيبويه: هما اسمان بنيا على الفتح كاسم واحد كخمسة عشر ونحوه

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة
rows.claim: The remaining canonical readers use a kasra on mīm; the Kufan analysis treats the form as inflected with the possessive yāʾ omitted and represented by kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة بكسر الميم فقياس قول الكوفيين أنه معرب وحذفت ياء المتكلم

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: For the kasra form, Sibawayh says it is built and attached to the possessive yāʾ, omitted with its kasra retained; an ordinary construct-state form could not drop the yāʾ because it is not itself vocative.
rows.anchor: وقال سيبويه هو مبني أضيف إلى ياء المتكلم كما قالوا يا أحد عشر أقبلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A recitation also retains the possessive yāʾ explicitly.
rows.anchor: وقرىء بإثبات ياء الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among the forms, the best is omitting the possessive yāʾ with its kasra retained; other possible forms change it to alif and vary the tāʾ and mīm vowels, including in related kinship calls.
rows.anchor: وأجود اللغات الاجتزاء بالكسرة عن ياء الإضافة ثم قلب الياء ألفا والكسرة قبلها فتحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other attested forms include yā ibn ummi with the yāʾ retained and ibn imi with kasra on hamza and mīm.
rows.anchor: وقرىء يا ابن أمي بإثبات الياء وابن إم بكسر الهمزة والميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vocative and the following sentence together complete what was said, to soften Moses' anger and excuse Aaron as having warned them as far as his strength allowed.
rows.anchor: ومعمول القول المنادى والجملة بعده المقصود بها تخفيف ما أدرك موسى من الغضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron's explanation shows he had not failed to admonish and warn; the people overpowered him and ignored his counsel, nearly killing him.
rows.anchor: ولكنهم استضعفوه فلم يلتفتوا إلى وعظه بل قاربوا أن يقتلوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istadaʿafūnī means they found or considered me weak, derived from the sense of finding something to be as its verbal root expresses.
rows.anchor: ومعنى استضعفوني وجدوني فهي بمعنى إلفاء الشيء بمعنى ما صيغ منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After explaining the people's oppression and near attempt to kill him, Aaron asks Moses not to make the enemies rejoice by harming him, which would make him blameworthy before both them and Moses.
rows.anchor: ولما أبدى له ما كان منهم من الاستضعاف له ومقاربة قتلهم إياه سأله ترك ما يسرهم بفعله

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poet says death is preferable to the enemies' gloating.
rows.anchor: والموت دون شماتة الأعداء

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muhaysin reads tashmat with fatḥa on tāʾ, kasra on mīm, and the enemies in the accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن تشمت بفتح التاء وكسر الميم ونصب الأعداء

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads tashmat with both tāʾ and mīm open and the enemies in the accusative.
rows.anchor: ومجاهد كذلك إلا أنه فتح الميم

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح
rows.claim: Abu al-Fath construes Mujahid's reading intransitively as a prayer that God not gloat, supplying an omitted verb for 'the enemies'; the author calls this strained because shamit is attested as transitive.
rows.anchor: وخرج أبو الفتح قراءة مجاهد على أن تكون لازمة والمعنى فلا تشمت أنت يا رب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Abu al-Fath's strained intransitive reading: shamit is reported as transitive, so no omitted verb is needed; the comparisons with God's mockery or plotting are replies to opponents, not initiated speech.
rows.anchor: وهذا خروج عن الظاهر وتكلف في الإعراب وقد روي تعدي شمت لغة فلا يتكلف أنها لازمة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also has tashmat with both vowels open and al-aʿdāʾ nominative, while Humayd ibn Qays has a kasra on mīm; they make the verb intransitive with enemies as its subject.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد فلا تشمت بفتح التاء والميم ورفع الأعداء، وعن حميد بن قيس كذلك إلا أنه كسر الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the intransitive readings, the surface wording tells the enemies not to gloat, while the intended plea to Aaron is not to expose Moses to harm that would make them rejoice.
rows.anchor: فظاهره أنه نهى الأعداء عن الشماتة به وهو من باب لا أرينك هنا والمراد نهيه أخاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron first asks that Moses not give the enemies a visible cause for gloating, then asks not to be judged or treated as one of the wrongdoers, a less visible inner judgment.
rows.anchor: وبدأ أولا بسؤال أخيه أن لا يشمت به الأعداء لأن ما يوجب الشماتة هو فعل مكروه ظاهر لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final plea can mean that Moses should not make Aaron a companion of the wrongdoers in his anger.
rows.anchor: أو يكون المعنى ولا تجعلني في موجدتك علي قرينا لهم مصاحبا لهم
